title: The Organizational Costs of Dysfunctional Leaders
author: Jason L. Zimmerman
summary: Jason Zimmerman argues that organizations become so skilled at accommodating difficult leaders that the cost of the behavior disappears from view. Teams build workarounds, extra meetings and defensive documentation, so contribution stays concentrated and visible while the costs are spread thinly across many people. He cites Tucker and Edmondson's study of nurses, who solved 93 percent of problems locally and so left the underlying system failures hidden. To surface the pattern, he recommends moving from individual opinions to collective evidence, using multisource feedback and Organizational Network Analysis questions in existing surveys. Because a diagnosis is not a verdict, he advises the least invasive intervention that fits, from coaching and support to role redesign, with separation as a last resort. The earlier the pattern is seen, the more options an organization has.
points: Accommodation works well enough that the person at the center of the dysfunction stays invisible to those with authority to act.
The 'contributes more than they cost' math is skewed because contribution is visible and concentrated while costs are distributed across teams.
Workarounds that go unexamined harden into 'just the way we do things around here', as the nurse study showed with 93 percent of problems solved locally.
Organizational Network Analysis questions can be added to existing surveys to reveal whom people trust, consult, or avoid.
Interventions should be the least invasive that fits, ranging from coaching and support to role redesign, with separation only when others fail.
quotes: Contribution is concentrated and visible, while the costs of accommodation are distributed across several people and even teams.
The problem is that these workarounds can make dysfunction surprisingly routine. And costly.
Over time, the people can become so good at accommodating the dysfunction that it becomes difficult to know where the cost originated.
The nurses did what capable people tend to do. They found a way through. In 93 percent of the problems observed, nurses solved the immediate issue rather than trying to change whatever had caused it.
Information, like water, tends to find the path of least resistance. People bring problems to those they trust and avoid those they do not.

Simply showing someone how others experience them produces only modest improvement on its own. Awareness is useful, but it usually needs to be paired with some form of development, support, or change in the environment around the person.

The advantage of seeing the pattern earlier is that it gives an organization more choices. Instead of waiting until frustration has hardened into resignation, bureaucracy, or turnover, leaders can intervene while the problem is still smaller and while the person at the center of it may still have room to change.
Which is why the denominator in the ROI calculation may be wrong. And the farther up the organization the dysfunction sits, the more expensive that accommodation can become.
